For a complete SMPS / converter design workflow, ON Semiconductor Design Tools are a good **starting point** (topology selection, controller selection, quick sizing). The missing pieces are usually: **high-fidelity simulation**, **control-loop work**, **magnetics**, **PCB/layout + parasitics**, and **thermal/EMI validation**.

## Recommended “next” tool (most leverage): **LTspice (SPICE simulator)**
**Why:** It complements ON’s calculators by letting you validate real switching behavior (start-up, protection events, ringing, loss/efficiency trends, stress on MOSFET/diode/capacitors) with parasitics and vendor models. It’s also widely used, free, and has strong community support.

**Strengths**
- Accurate time-domain switching simulation with real device models (when available).
- Great for “what-if” changes (snubbers, gate resistors, diode selection, RC damping, layout parasitic estimates).
- Parameter sweeps and Monte Carlo help with tolerance/corner cases.

**Limitations**
- Can be slow for long transients or complex converters (especially with detailed magnetics and tight timesteps).
- Results depend heavily on model quality (controllers often have simplified/behavioral models).
- Control-loop design is possible but not as streamlined as dedicated loop tools.

> If you routinely simulate large, complex power stages and need speed: consider **SIMPLIS/SIMetrix** (much faster for switching SMPS). If you need system/control co-simulation: consider **PLECS**.

## Complementary tools to complete the workflow (by design phase)

### 1) Control-loop / compensation
- **Tool:** RidleyWorks, Venable, or MATLAB (Control System Toolbox)
- **Use:** Plant modeling, compensator design, phase margin/gain margin, crossover targets, Bode plots, current-mode subharmonic checks.
- **Limitations:** Commercial tools cost; MATLAB requires setup; still needs real-world validation.

### 2) Magnetics design (inductor/transformer)
- **Tool:** **FEMM** (free 2D FEM) + vendor core tools (Magnetics Inc., Würth, TDK calculators)
- **Use:** Core selection, gap sizing, saturation margin, copper loss, fringing, leakage estimation.
- **Limitations:** FEMM is 2D (not perfect for complex geometries); transformer interwinding capacitance and EMI are tricky.

### 3) PCB design + library management
- **Tool:** **KiCad** (free) or **Altium Designer** (industry standard)
- **Use:** Layout, creepage/clearance, via current capability, footprint control, test points, variants.
- **Limitations:** Needs disciplined library/process; layout quality dominates EMI/thermal outcomes.

### 4) Thermal analysis
- **Tool:** Simcenter Flotherm / ANSYS Icepak (high-end) or simpler: SimScale + spreadsheet thermal network
- **Use:** MOSFET/diode/inductor hot spots, airflow sensitivity, heatsink selection, enclosure constraints.
- **Limitations:** Accuracy depends on boundary conditions; early-stage models are approximate.

### 5) EMI/EMC pre-compliance
- **Tool:** Near-field probe set + spectrum analyzer (or EMI receiver) + LISN; optional: CST/ANSYS HFSS for advanced modeling
- **Use:** Identify hot loops, common-mode noise sources, filter tuning, shielding/ground strategy validation.
- **Limitations:** Full-wave simulation is heavy; practical EMI success is mostly layout + measurement iteration.

### 6) Component sourcing + footprints
- **Tool:** Octopart + SnapEDA/Ultra Librarian
- **Use:** Alternate parts, lifecycle risk, parametric filtering, footprint/model sourcing.
- **Limitations:** Always verify footprints against datasheets; don’t trust symbols blindly.

### 7) Lab validation (cannot be skipped for SMPS)
- **Tools:** Scope + **differential probe**, current probe, electronic load, thermal camera/IR thermometer, LCR meter, power analyzer (optional but valuable)
- **Use:** Validate stability, ripple, transient response, efficiency, stress, thermal, EMI.
- **Limitations:** Probe technique and grounding errors can completely mislead results.

## A practical end-to-end workflow (with ON Semi tools as the front end)

1) **Architecture & part selection (ON Semi Design Tools)**
   - Choose topology, controller, switching frequency, rough magnetics/cap sizing.
   - Capture initial BOM targets and operating points.

2) **Detailed electrical simulation (LTspice / SIMPLIS)**
   - Build full schematic with realistic parasitics (input loop ESL, switch node capacitance, gate loop inductance).
   - Check: start-up, OCP/OVP behavior, switching stress, ringing, snubber needs, loss trends.

3) **Control-loop design (Ridley/MATLAB or in-sim Bode)**
   - Derive plant (or average model), design compensation, validate phase margin across line/load/temp.
   - Confirm transient response targets.

4) **Magnetics design (FEMM + vendor tools)**
   - Verify saturation margin at worst-case current/temp.
   - Estimate copper/core loss and temperature rise.
   - Iterate inductance and ripple targets if losses/size are off.

5) **PCB layout (KiCad/Altium)**
   - Place/route with priority: high di/dt loops, switch node containment, Kelvin sensing, gate drive loop.
   - Add measurement points (switch node, gate, current sense, COMP/FB, input/output ripple).

6) **Thermal & EMI iterations (thermal tool + pre-compliance measurements)**
   - Tune copper/heatsinking/airflow; adjust snubbers and filters.
   - Validate against target standards early if productized.

7) **Prototype bring-up & correlation**
   - Correlate waveform shapes, losses, loop stability, and temperatures back to simulation.
   - Update parasitics/models to match reality for the next spin.

## Practical tips (things that save weeks)
- **Model realism:** Add *explicit* parasitics (ESR/ESL of caps, trace inductance, diode Qrr, MOSFET Coss, gate resistance). Most “it works in sim” failures are parasitic-related.
- **Sim in layers:** Use an **average model** for loop work + a **switching model** for stress/EMI/ringing.
- **Design for measurement:** Put in pads for RC snubbers, gate resistors, and filter components so you can tune without re-spinning the PCB.
- **Probe correctly:** Use a spring ground or coax pigtail for switch-node/ripple; avoid long ground leads (they fabricate ringing).
- **Loop stability verification:** Plan to measure Bode (injection transformer) or at least validate via load steps across line/load/temp.
- **Layout is a “circuit element”:** Treat the hot loops as components; minimize loop area first, then worry about “pretty routing”.

- Licensed tool (cost). If budget is tight, consider alternatives below.

**Good lower-cost/free alternatives (depending on your needs):**
- **LTspice** (free): excellent for many SMPS sims; may be slower/less robust for complex switching + long transients.

- **PSIM**: very popular for power electronics; fast and practical for converters and motor drives.

**Tool options:** Ansys Icepak, Simcenter Flotherm, or simpler: heatsink spreadsheets + measured θ values  
- **Strengths:** predicts hot spots, airflow sensitivity, enclosure effects.
- **Limitations:** needs good boundary conditions; early results can be misleading without calibration.

- **Near-term practical:** spectrum analyzer + LISN (hardware), near-field probes

- **Strengths:** reduces surprise failures late in the cycle.

**Tool options:** MATLAB/Simulink, Control System Toolbox, or dedicated loop tools (RidleyWorks), plus Monte Carlo in SIMPLIS/PSIM where available  
- **Strengths:** loop stability, transient tuning, plant modeling, sensitivity analysis.
- **Limitations:** model fidelity matters; measured plant validation is still important.

### F) Test/validation instrumentation (often the real bottleneck)
**Minimum “serious SMPS” lab set:**
- Oscilloscope with **differential probe** + **current probe**
- Electronic load, programmable supply
- **Power analyzer** (or at least good DMMs + shunts) for efficiency
- **LISN + spectrum analyzer** for conducted EMI pre-checks
- Thermal camera or thermocouples

8) **Design freeze + compliance + production**
   - DFM/DFT checks, component availability (Octopart/SiliconExpert), finalize test plan.

## 4) Practical tips (what usually saves the most time)
- **Simulate with parasitics early** (input cap ESL, package inductance, diode Qrr, transformer leakage) or your first prototype will “discover” them for you.
- **Treat layout as part of the circuit**: minimize the hot loop area (switch–diode/sync FET–input caps), keep gate drive tight, and control return currents.
- **Design for measurement**: include loop injection point, sense resistor options, RC snubber pads, and EMI filter stuffing options.
- **Don’t trust a single model**: cross-check controller behavior using (1) vendor reference design, (2) your simulator, and (3) bench waveforms.
- **Plan EMI from day 1**: leave space for a common-mode choke, extra Y-cap footprint options, and an input damping network.

- **Why:** SMPS success often hinges on switching-node containment, input filtering, and return paths—best validated with bench pre-scan.

- **Current probe**, **electronic load**, **power analyzer**, **thermal camera/thermocouples**
- **Why:** You must confirm switch-node ringing, peak currents, loss distribution, efficiency, and thermal margins.

- **Design in tuning hooks:** footprints for snubber RC, optional gate resistors, ferrite beads, alternate compensation components.

- **Corner the design early:** min VIN/max load and max VIN/light load are common stress/EMI corners.

## Practical tips (things that most often bite 12 V → 3.3 V bucks)

- **Minimum on-time vs switching frequency:** at high fSW, 12→3.3 can push Ton(min). If you see duty-cycle limiting or skipped pulses, reduce fSW or choose a part with lower Ton(min).
- **Inductor selection:** don’t just match inductance—check **Isat at temperature** and **DCR loss**. Many “mystery” thermal issues are inductor copper loss.
- **Capacitor derating:** MLCCs at 3.3 V bias lose capacitance; ensure effective Cout meets transient needs.
- **Input capacitor placement:** the **VIN–HSFET–LSFET/diode–GND loop** is the EMI/overshoot hotspot. Place the input ceramic cap *tight* to the IC power pins.
- **Switch node discipline:** keep SW copper small, avoid running it near feedback/comp nets, and avoid planes under SW if EMI is tight.
- **Compensation and load steps:** if the tool “auto-compensates,” still validate worst-case (cold/hot, min/max Vin, min/max load). If possible, verify with a Bode measurement on the prototype.
- **Ringing control:** if SW ringing is high, consider an **RC snubber** (sized from measured ringing frequency) rather than guessing.

## Practical tips (things that materially improve SMPS simulation quality)

- **Start with the vendor reference design values** (including compensation) before optimizing—reduces “false instability” caused by unrealistic assumptions.
- **Add parasitics early:**  
  - Inductor DCR, capacitor ESR/ESL, MOSFET package inductance, and a few nH in the hot loop.  
  This is often the difference between “no ringing” and “realistic ringing.”
- **Control the timestep:** For hard-switching waveforms, limit max timestep to capture edges/ringing; otherwise you can get misleading peak currents/voltages.
- **Use measured magnetics when possible:** If you have inductor core loss data or at least saturation curves, include them (current limit behavior can change drastically).
- **Validate at the “pain corners”:** minimum VIN + maximum load, maximum VIN + light load, and cold/hot component shifts (ESR changes a lot with temperature).
- **Don’t trust a single simulator outcome:** If a result is borderline (stability margin, peak VDS, diode stress), re-check with a second approach (e.g., PSpice detailed transient + SIMPLIS loop analysis).

## Practical tips (to avoid common verification traps)

- **Model realism:** Add parasitics intentionally (ESR/ESL of caps, DCR of inductor, diode Qrr, MOSFET package inductance). “Ideal parts” hide instability and ringing.  
- **Probe like you mean it:** Bad probing can make a stable design look unstable (or hide ringing). Use short grounds and proper differential probing.  
- **Verify at corners:** Minimum Vin + maximum load is often worst for duty cycle/current; maximum Vin can be worst for switching loss and OVP behavior.  
- **Check protection behavior explicitly:** Short-circuit response, hiccup timing, restart conditions, and thermal behavior are frequent “gotchas.”  
- **Don’t trust compensation blindly:** Even if PSWD suggests a compensation network, confirm phase margin in at least one analytical or measured way.  
- **Layout is part of the circuit:** If your sim lacks layout parasitics, assume you’ll need snubbers/RC damping options and leave footprints.

## Practical tips to get real efficiency gains
- **Optimize to your load profile**, not just “peak efficiency at full load.” Many products care more about 10–40% load.
- Watch the **frequency trade**:
  - Higher fSW → smaller magnetics but often worse switching loss
  - Lower fSW → better switching loss but can increase ripple current and magnetics size/core loss
- Include **magnetics loss explicitly**: in many designs, “efficiency optimization” that ignores core loss picks an fSW that looks great on paper but underperforms thermally.
- Check operating mode at light load (**PFM/skip/burst**). It can boost light-load efficiency but may impact ripple/EMI—decide early.
- Don’t forget “small” losses that add up:
  - Input/output capacitor ESR ripple heating
  - Sense resistor loss (or choose lossless sensing)
  - Gate-drive loss (Qg × Vdrive × fSW)
- Plan for **layout-dependent efficiency**: loop inductance can increase ringing → more switching loss → more snubbing → more loss. Keep high di/dt loops tight from the start.

1. **Optimize for the actual load profile**

2. **Always separate losses into buckets**
   - MOSFET conduction, MOSFET switching (incl. Coss/Eoss), gate-drive, diode/body-diode, inductor copper, inductor core, sense/driver/aux supply, snubbers/clamps.
   - The “biggest bar” in the loss chart tells you what to change next.

   - Many designs leave large efficiency on the table by choosing Fsw too high “for size” without quantifying thermal cost, or too low and paying in magnetics conduction loss/ripple.

   - Core loss vs copper loss trade is frequently the difference between “good” and “great” efficiency—especially at higher Fsw.
5. **Validate deadtime assumptions**
   - Deadtime that’s slightly off can dominate losses (body diode conduction) in synchronous converters.
6. **Use relative comparisons early, absolute accuracy later**
   - Early: use PLECS to rank design choices and find sensitivities.  
   - Late: calibrate with measured switching energies/temps for accurate absolute efficiency prediction.

### Phase 0 — Requirements capture (the “contract”)
**Inputs you must lock down**
- Input range (min/nom/max), surges, UVLO/OVP expectations
- Output(s): voltage accuracy, current, peak load, load profile
- Transient response targets (ΔV, recovery time), allowable ripple/noise
- Efficiency targets and operating temperature range
- Size/height constraints, cost targets, production volume
- EMI/EMC targets (CISPR class, automotive OEM limits, etc.)
- Safety/isolation requirements (if offline): creepage/clearance, standards
- Protections: OCP/short, OTP, OVP, reverse polarity, inrush, etc.

**Deliverable**
- One-page spec + an “edge conditions” table (min/max everything).

---

### Phase 1 — Topology and architecture selection
**Decide**
- Buck / boost / buck-boost / flyback / LLC / forward / active clamp, etc.
- Synchronous vs. diode rectification
- Switching frequency target (tradeoff: size vs. efficiency/EMI)
- Current sensing method (shunt, inductor DCR, valley/peak, etc.)
- Need for spread-spectrum, synchronization, soft-start behavior

**Tools**
- onsemi design guides/reference designs to shortlist workable architectures
- Quick hand calcs / spreadsheet for power stage sanity

**Deliverable**
- Chosen topology + rough switching frequency + control method rationale.

**Use onsemi tools to**
- Select controller/regulator meeting: VIN range, VOUT, IOUT, frequency, features (sync FET drive, current-mode, etc.)
- Pull **reference designs** nearest your operating point
- Check **package thermal capability**, gate drive current, sense thresholds, minimum on-time/off-time constraints

**Complementary checks**
- MOSFET selection: conduction + switching losses across VIN/VOUT corners
- Diode selection (if async): reverse recovery, Vf vs. temperature
- Inductor choice: saturation current at peak, core loss at chosen fSW
- Capacitors: ripple current rating, ESR/ESL, DC bias derating (MLCC)

**Deliverable**
- Candidate IC + preliminary BOM (power train, magnetics, caps, sense).

### Phase 3 — First-pass design synthesis (sizing + stress)
**Do the “corner math”**
- Duty cycle extremes, inductor ripple ratio (ΔIL), peak switch current
- Worst-case RMS currents in input/output caps
- Switch-node voltage overshoot risk (layout + parasitics assumption)
- Snubber needs estimate (RC/RCD) if applicable
- Thermal budget: estimate losses and junction temps

**Tools**
- onsemi calculators/design assistants (where available)
- Spreadsheet with corner cases and derating

**Deliverable**
- “Design summary” table: stresses, ratings, margins, expected efficiency.

### Phase 4 — Simulation and loop stability verification
**Goal:** catch instability, excessive ringing, and startup/protection surprises before PCB.

**Recommended simulation stack**
1. **Vendor SPICE / PSpice** (with onsemi macromodels)  
   - Validate start-up, steady-state waveforms, switch stress, basic transients.
2. **SIMPLIS (or equivalent switching-focused simulator)** *(highly recommended if you have access)*  
   - Much faster for SMPS steady-state + load steps + control loop work.
3. **LTspice** *(free alternative if models available/compatible)*  
   - Good for power stage and parasitic ringing exploration, snubber tuning.

**What to simulate**
- Startup into load, soft-start, pre-bias behavior
- Load steps (min→max, max→min), recovery, overshoot/undershoot
- Line steps (VIN min↔max)
- Current limit behavior and short-circuit response
- Compensation sweep / loop gain (or AC injection method if supported)
- Component tolerances: ESR shifts, L value, sense resistor, etc.

**Deliverable**
- Simulation report: waveforms + loop margins (gain/phase margin targets).

### Phase 5 — EMI and input/output filter planning (pre-layout)
**Design intent**
- Define input EMI filter topology (CM/DM as needed), damping strategy
- Output ripple target: choose LC/π filtering, check control interaction
- Plan for snubbers, RC damping, ferrite beads (only when justified)

**Tools**
- Spreadsheet + basic SPICE for filter resonance/damping
- Plan measurement approach early (LISN, near-field probe)

**Deliverable**
- Filter schematic with damping elements and expected corner behavior.

### Phase 6 — PCB layout (this is where SMPS succeed or fail)
**Layout priorities**
- Minimize high di/dt loops:  
  - Input cap ↔ high-side FET ↔ low-side FET/diode ↔ return
  - Switch node area small; keep it away from feedback/sense
- Kelvin sense for current sense resistor and output voltage sense
- Solid ground strategy (power ground vs. signal ground with controlled tie point)
- Place compensation/FB parts tight to IC; guard against switch-node coupling
- Thermal: copper pours, vias, heat spreading; airflow assumptions
- Provide test points for: SW node, gate, VIN, VOUT, COMP/FB, sense nodes

**Tools**
- PCB CAD: Altium/KiCad/OrCAD
- Optional: field solver/PDN tools for high-current planes
- onsemi layout guidelines from datasheets/reference layouts

**Deliverable**
- Layout review checklist + annotated critical loops screenshot.

### Phase 7 — Prototype build plan (reduce re-spin risk)
**Prototype strategy**
- Build **2–3 variants** if possible (snubber footprints, optional RC damping pads, alt compensation components)
- Stuff options for key parts: gate resistors, bootstrap diode, sense filter RC, RC snubber pads
- Choose accurate current measurement points (shunt footprint or coax loop)

**Deliverable**
- “Bring-up BOM” and assembly notes (do-not-populate options).

---

### Phase 8 — Bring-up and bench validation (structured, repeatable)
**Power-up sequence**
- Start with current-limited supply (if applicable) or series resistor
- Check gate drive, soft-start ramp, VOUT regulation at light load
- Increase load gradually; monitor switch node and current waveforms
- Verify protections: OCP, short-circuit, UVLO/OVP, thermal (if feasible)

**Core tests**
- Efficiency map vs. VIN and load
- Ripple/noise (bandwidth-limited measurement techniques)
- Load transient response (step load with controlled slew)
- Thermal soak at worst-case conditions
- Stability spot checks (Bode if you have injection transformer setup)

**Tools**
- Oscilloscope + differential probe + current probe
- Electronic load
- Power analyzer (preferred for efficiency)
- Thermal camera or thermocouples
- LISN + spectrum analyzer (or pre-compliance EMI receiver)

**Deliverable**
- Test report with plots, pass/fail vs. original spec, and action items.

- Refine filter damping to avoid peaking

## Practical tips (things that prevent the most common failures)
1. **Start from the closest onsemi reference design** and only change one major variable at a time (VIN range, fSW, power level).
2. **Design for measurement**: add coax-friendly loop points for current probing, and pads for injection/compensation tweaks.
3. **Over-derate magnetics and MLCCs**: inductor saturation and MLCC DC-bias derating are frequent “it worked in sim” failures.
4. **Plan damping early**: every LC you add (input filter, output filter) risks resonances that destabilize control loops.
5. **Layout is part of the circuit**: treat parasitics as components—keep hot loops tight and sensitive nodes shielded.
6. **Corner validation beats nominal success**: test VIN min/max, load min/max, cold/hot, and worst-case combinations.
7. **EMI is iterative**: expect at least one loop of snubber/gate/filter/layout refinement before you’re happy.

## Complete SMPS design workflow (spec → prototype), using onsemi tools + complementary tools

### 0) Inputs you must lock down (specification checklist)
Capture in a single spec sheet (Excel/Sheets works fine):
- **Input:** min/nom/max, surges, UVLO/OVLO, source impedance, hold-up requirements
- **Output:** voltage tolerance, max load, load range, ripple/noise targets, transient (load step size & recovery)
- **Efficiency & thermal:** target efficiency, ambient range, airflow, max case/board temps
- **Protection:** OCP (cycle-by-cycle vs latch), OVP, OTP, SCP behavior
- **Isolation & safety (if isolated):** working voltage, creepage/clearance, standards (IEC 62368-1 etc.)
- **EMI/EMC:** CISPR class target, conducted/radiated expectations, switching frequency constraints
- **Mechanical & cost:** height limits, inductor/transformer constraints, BOM cost target

**Output of this step:** a one-page “SMPS requirements” document plus test conditions.

---

### 1) Topology selection (architecture)
Choose based on input/output ratio, isolation, power level:
- **Non-isolated:** buck, boost, buck-boost, SEPIC, Ćuk
- **Isolated:** flyback (low–mid power), forward, LLC (higher power, high efficiency), active clamp flyback

**Complementary tools:**
- Quick trade studies: spreadsheet + basic power-stage equations
- If dynamics matter early: **PLECS** or **PSIM** for system-level behavior (optional)

**Output:** chosen topology + rough switching frequency range + control mode preference (voltage mode/current mode/peak current, etc.).

---

### 2) First-pass design in onsemi tools (controller/device selection + component sizing)
Use onsemi Power Supply Design Tools / WebDesigner to:
- Select a **controller/regulator IC** that matches:
  - input range and gate drive needs
  - synchronous vs diode rectification
  - current sensing method (sense resistor, DCR, current transformer)
  - protections and soft-start behavior
- Generate/suggest:
  - **inductor/transformer target** (L, peak current)
  - **output capacitor** range (C, ESR/ESL targets)
  - **compensation network starting values**
  - **MOSFET/diode ratings** and rough losses

**Output:** initial schematic + BOM + operating point estimates.

---

### 3) Magnetics design (often the make-or-break step)
**Non-isolated (inductor):**
- Verify saturation current margin (include ripple + transient + tolerance)
- Choose core/material for loss at your **fsw** and ripple

**Isolated (transformer/flyback):**
- Select turns ratio, primary inductance, peak current, demag margin
- Plan for leakage inductance and snubber/clamp needs

**Complementary tools:**
- Vendor tools: **Würth REDEXPERT**, **Coilcraft selector**, **Magnetics Inc. design resources**
- If you’re building custom magnetics: a magnetics spreadsheet + (optional) **ANSYS Maxwell** for deeper work

**Output:** a magnetics spec (L, Isat, DCR; or transformer turns, gap, wire, bobbin, insulation system).

---

### 4) Detailed simulation (electrical + control loop)
Take the onsemi schematic and:
- Use **PSpice (Cadence) / onsemi SPICE models** (or LTspice if models are compatible) to validate:
  - steady-state regulation across line/load
  - switch node behavior (ringing, overshoot)
  - start-up/shutdown sequencing
  - protection triggers (OCP/OVP behavior)

**Loop stability:**
- Do **AC injection** simulation where possible (Bode plot)
- Target typical margins (rule of thumb): **phase margin ~45–60°**, gain margin > 6–10 dB (adjust to your transient goals)

**Complementary tools (often superior for switching convergence):**
- **SIMPLIS** (very strong for SMPS stability/transient with switching efficiency)
- **PSIM** (good for power electronics, faster than SPICE for many cases)

**Output:** validated component values + compensation tuned + identified snubber/clamp needs.

---

### 5) Loss/thermal estimation (before layout)
Build a loss budget:
- MOSFET: conduction + switching + gate drive
- Diode/rectifier: conduction + reverse recovery (if applicable)
- Inductor/transformer: copper + core loss
- IC: quiescent + gate drive + internal switch loss (if integrated)

**Complementary tools:**
- Spreadsheet loss budget (recommended even if tools provide estimates)
- Thermal: **ANSYS Icepak / FloTHERM** (optional), or conservative θJA/θJC-based estimates

**Output:** worst-case temperatures and where you need copper, vias, heatsinking, airflow, or a different package.

---

### 6) EMI-risk design pass (before PCB)
Do not wait for the lab to “discover” EMI.
- Identify hot loops:
  - input cap ↔ high-side switch ↔ return
  - switch node ↔ rectifier ↔ output cap
- Plan filtering:
  - input π-filter (mind impedance interaction)
  - CM choke needs (isolated offline designs)
- Plan damping:
  - RC snubber, RCD clamp, active clamp tuning

**Complementary tools:**
- SPICE for input filter + damping
- If you have access: pre-layout parasitic estimation, or at least rule-based layout constraints

**Output:** EMI strategy + placeholder footprints for snubbers/ferrites/RC positions.

---

### 7) PCB layout (treat as a design phase, not a clerical step)
Use Altium/KiCad/etc., but follow SMPS rules:
- Minimize **high di/dt loop areas**
- Keep switch node copper **small** (but not so small you overheat)
- Kelvin-sense current sense resistors and feedback nodes
- Solid ground strategy (power ground vs signal ground, single-point tie where appropriate)
- Place input/output ceramics tight to the power stage pins
- Add test points for: SW, COMP, FB, CS, VCC, GND (and primary/secondary grounds if isolated)

**Best practice with onsemi ecosystem:**
- Start from an **onsemi EVM/reference layout** if available for the same controller.

**Output:** PCB ready for fabrication + assembly notes.

---

### 8) Prototype bring-up (risk-controlled)
Recommended bench setup:
- Current-limited supply or pre-charge
- Electronic load
- Oscilloscope with proper probing (spring ground, diff probe for high-side if needed)
- Current probe (or sense resistor temporarily)
- Thermal camera/thermocouples

Bring-up sequence:
1. Power IC bias only (if separable), verify VCC/UVLO
2. No-load start, confirm switching frequency and soft-start
3. Low load, validate regulation and ripple
4. Step loads (transient response)
5. Line sweep + load sweep (watch OCP/OVP)
6. Thermal soak at worst-case conditions
7. EMI pre-scan (LISN + spectrum analyzer) before formal testing

**Output:** a controlled set of waveforms + pass/fail log per requirement.

---

### 9) Debug/iterate (the normal loop)
Typical iteration triggers:
- Ringing/overshoot → adjust snubber, layout, gate resistance, clamp
- Poor transient/instability → re-tune compensation, adjust output caps/ESR zero, verify current-sense filtering
- Thermal hotspots → redistribute copper, add vias/heatsink, lower fsw, upgrade MOSFET/inductor
- EMI failures → tighten loops, add CM/DM filtering, slow edges carefully, improve shielding/return paths

- Efficiency targets at key operating points, standby power.

**Complementary tools:** requirements template (Markdown/Docs), test plan spreadsheet.

---

### 1) Topology selection + architecture
**Deliverables:** topology choice + block diagram + switching frequency plan.
- Non-isolated: buck/boost/buck-boost/SEPIC.
- Isolated: flyback (low–mid power), forward/active clamp, LLC (higher efficiency at higher power).
- Decide: synchronous vs diode rectification, current-mode vs voltage-mode, fixed vs quasi-resonant, CCM/DCM/CrCM.

**onsemi inputs:** controller families + app notes to validate topology suitability.

---

### 2) First-pass power stage sizing (hand calcs)
**Deliverables:** initial component values + stress table.
- Inductor/transformer target ripple current, saturation margin.
- Peak/valley currents, sense resistor sizing, current-limit margins.
- MOSFET/diode voltage/current stress with margin (including ringing).
- Output capacitor sizing (ripple + transient + ESR/ESL).
- Input capacitor RMS current rating.
- Switching frequency trade-off: size vs efficiency vs EMI.

**Complementary tools:** spreadsheet (Excel/Sheets) for corner sweeps (VIN min/max, load min/max, temp).

---

### 3) Part selection in onsemi ecosystem
**Deliverables:** controller choice + semiconductors + preliminary BOM.
- Use onsemi parametric search to choose controller meeting:
  - control method, frequency range, gate drive strength, protection set, soft-start, sync, spread-spectrum, etc.
- Choose FETs/rectifiers (onsemi or otherwise) based on:
  - conduction + switching loss estimates, SOA, Qg, reverse recovery, package thermal.
- Choose gate driver (if needed), current sense method (shunt, DCR, sense FET), feedback (opto/secondary ref for isolated).

**onsemi tools/collateral:** reference schematics, datasheet “typical application,” design notes, SPICE models.

---

### 4) Control-loop design (stability and transient behavior)
**Deliverables:** compensation network + predicted phase margin/gain margin.
- Determine power-stage small-signal model (buck/boost differs; isolated adds RHP zero considerations).
- Design Type II/III compensation (or opto+TL431 style network for isolated).
- Ensure stability across:
  - VIN extremes, load extremes, capacitor tolerance/aging, temperature, CCM/DCM boundaries.
- Plan measurement method for prototype (injection transformer, FRA/Bode).

**Complementary tools (recommended):**
- Control loop: MATLAB/Octave, Python control toolbox, or dedicated loop tools.
- Simulation: SPICE AC analysis with averaged model where practical.

---

### 5) Switching simulation (waveforms, stress, losses)
**Deliverables:** simulated switching node ringing, peak currents/voltages, loss breakdown.
- Use onsemi SPICE models for controller/FET/diode when available.
- Verify:
  - switch node overshoot/ringing, diode recovery stress,
  - current limit behavior, startup, short-circuit,
  - snubber impact, dead-time (sync designs),
  - efficiency estimate and hotspot prediction inputs.

**Complementary tools:** LTspice / PSpice (depending on model compatibility), plus a loss spreadsheet for sanity checks.

---

### 6) Magnetics design (inductor/transformer)
**Deliverables:** magnetic design spec + vendor part or custom winding drawing.
- Core selection, AL, air gap, flux density margin at worst-case.
- Copper loss (skin/proximity), fill, thermal rise.
- Leakage inductance + interwinding capacitance (critical for flyback EMI and ringing).
- Plan for **measured** inductance/leakage verification on prototypes.

**Complementary tools:** vendor magnetic calculators (e.g., Würth REDEXPERT or core vendor tools), plus LCR meter validation plan.

---

### 7) EMI/EMC strategy (designed-in, not patched later)
**Deliverables:** EMI plan + filter placeholders + layout constraints.
- Partition noise sources: input current loops, switch node dv/dt, transformer capacitance, rectifier recovery.
- Design input filter with damping (avoid filter-control interaction).
- Add footprints for:
  - RC/RCD snubbers, ferrite beads, split resistors for gate, CM choke options.
- Plan measurement: LISN for conducted, near-field probes for debug.

**Complementary tools:** EMI precompliance receiver/spectrum analyzer, LISN, near-field probe set.

---

### 8) Thermal design
**Deliverables:** worst-case junction temps with margin.
- Build a loss budget: FET, diode, magnetics, controller, sense resistor.
- Translate losses → temperature rise using package θJA/θJC + copper/heatsink assumptions.
- Decide heatsink vs copper spreading vs airflow requirements.

**Complementary tools:** simple thermal spreadsheet first; then CFD/thermal tools if power density is high.

---

### 9) Schematic capture + PCB layout (critical step for SMPS success)
**Deliverables:** layout that preserves the assumptions in your sims.
Key layout rules (most common failure point):
- Minimize **high di/dt loops** (input cap ↔ FET ↔ diode/return).
- Keep switch node copper small; avoid coupling into feedback.
- Use **Kelvin sensing** for current sense resistors and output sense.
- Separate noisy power ground from analog ground; join at a controlled point.
- Place bootstrap, gate resistor, and driver loop tightly.
- Provide test points: SW, gate, sense, VOUT, COMP, FB, RT/SS.
- For isolated: creepage/clearance, slots, Y-cap placement strategy.

**Complementary tools:** Altium/KiCad + field-solver/PDN tools if needed.

---

### 10) Prototype bring-up (safe and fast)
**Deliverables:** measured waveforms + first functional unit.
Bring-up sequence:
1. Visual inspection, continuity checks, verify component orientations.
2. Power with current-limited supply (or series power resistor for offline designs).
3. Verify controller bias rails, UVLO thresholds, soft-start behavior.
4. Check gate waveform (amplitude, ringing), then switch node.
5. Validate current sense (no false trips), then load-step testing.
6. Only after stable operation: push to worst-case VIN/load/temperature.

**Must-have lab tools:** differential probe, current probe, isolated probing strategy, electronic load, FRA (or network analyzer), thermal camera/thermocouples.

---

### 11) Debug → iterate → engineering prototype
**Deliverables:** Rev B/C improvements addressing EMI/thermal/transients.
- Tune compensation from measured Bode.
- Adjust snubbers/gate resistance to trade EMI vs efficiency.
- Refine magnetics if saturation, audible noise, or thermal issues appear.
- Fix layout coupling issues (often FB noise and ground impedance).

---

### 12) Pre-compliance validation
**Deliverables:** evidence you can pass formal test.
- Conducted EMI scans with LISN across line/load.
- Radiated quick checks with near-field + chamber time if available.
- ESD/EFT surge strategy (TVS, RC, layout return paths).
- Safety checks for isolated designs.

## Practical tips (that save time in open-source SMPS simulation)

1) **Use the right integration method for switching**
- In ngspice, **`method=gear`** often behaves better for power converters than default trapezoidal.
- Keep a tight leash on timestep (but not absurdly small); switching sims can lie if timestep is too large.

2) **Add “real-world friction” to help convergence**
- Add small series resistances (milliohms) to ideal L/C, small gate resistances, ESR/ESL.
- Avoid ideal voltage sources directly across ideal capacitors/inductors without some resistance.

3) **Stage complexity**
- First run: ideal switches + averaged control.
- Second run: real switch models, add parasitics.
- Third run: snubbers, clamps, gate drive details.

4) **Model import discipline**
- Prefer **unencrypted PSpice subcircuits** when possible.
- Expect to edit:
  - behavioral syntax (`B` sources, `table()`, `if()` differences)
  - .param usage and functions
  - unsupported elements
- Keep a small “model compatibility patch” file per vendor/model.

5) **Measure what matters using `.meas`**
- Automate extraction: peak switch current/voltage, ripple, average input/output power, efficiency estimate (with caution).

## Recommended tool: **PLECS (Stand-alone or Blockset)** — for efficiency + electro‑thermal analysis  
**Why:** In an SMPS workflow, “power efficiency” is fundamentally a **loss breakdown** problem (switching + conduction + magnetics + gate drive + snubbers), and “thermal” is those losses pushed through a **thermal network** (or CFD later). PLECS is purpose-built to (1) compute losses accurately and quickly across operating points and (2) propagate them into junction/case/heatsink temperatures with electro‑thermal simulation.

## Strengths vs. limitations

### Strengths
- **Fast power loss/efficiency sweeps:** line/load sweeps, deadtime sweeps, frequency sweeps, etc., without painfully slow transistor-level SPICE everywhere.
- **Detailed semiconductor loss models:** switching + conduction losses with parameterization; good for comparing MOSFETs/diodes and control choices.
- **Electro‑thermal coupling:** temperatures affect losses (Rds(on), Vf, etc.) and you can iterate to steady state or run transients.
- **Great for architecture decisions:** topology comparisons, synchronous vs. diode, snubber tradeoffs, frequency/inductor sizing impacts on loss.

### Limitations
- **Controller IC behavior isn’t always “drop‑in”:** you may need a simplified control model or co-simulate when exact PWM IC internal details matter.
- **Thermal network ≠ full CFD:** it’s excellent for junction/case/heatsink stackups, but not a replacement for PCB/enclosure airflow modeling.
- **Model quality matters:** you’ll still need vendor curves/models (Qg, Coss, reverse recovery, Rds(on) vs T, core loss data) to avoid false confidence.

## Practical tips to get better efficiency + thermal answers
- **Define an operating matrix early:** (Vin min/typ/max) × (Iout light/nom/max) × (Tamb) × (airflow). Most “surprises” occur off-nominal.
- **Treat datasheet RθJA cautiously:** it’s usually based on a JEDEC test board. For real designs, prefer **RθJC + board/heatsink model** (or 3D thermal sim).
- **Model temperature feedback in losses:** FET Rds(on) rises with temperature → more loss → higher Tj (positive feedback). Iterate losses at elevated temperature.
- **Don’t ignore “small” losses that become dominant at light load:**
  - gate-drive, controller bias, bootstrap losses, snubber bleed, clamp networks
- **Validate switching loss with realistic waveforms:** ringing/overshoot and slower edges can move switching energy a lot vs idealized assumptions.
- **Layout is an efficiency & thermal tool:**
  - minimize hot-loop inductance (reduces ringing and switching loss)
  - use Kelvin sensing where applicable
  - add thermal vias under hot packages; use copper spreading intentionally

## Strengths vs limitations

### Strengths
- **Fast loss/efficiency estimates** vs full SPICE transient switching runs (easy sweeps over Vin/Vout/Iout/fsw/deadtime).
- **Loss breakdown** (MOSFET conduction, switching, diode reverse recovery, magnetics copper/core, capacitor ESR, etc. depending on your models).
- **Electro-thermal loop**: apply losses → compute junction/case temps via RC thermal networks/heatsinks → update temperature-dependent parameters.
- **Control + power stage together** (helps you evaluate light-load modes, burst/skip, deadtime impact, etc.).

### Limitations / gotchas
- **Model fidelity depends on inputs**: datasheet-based loss models can miss layout-dependent parasitics, ringing, and real gate-drive behavior.
- **Not a replacement for layout-level thermal**: it won’t “see” hotspots caused by copper geometry, airflow, enclosure constraints.
- **Licensing cost** (vs LTspice/PSpice which are often free/low-cost).

## Practical tips (high leverage for efficiency + thermal)
- **Don’t trust a single operating point.** Build an operating-point matrix (Vin × Iout × ambient × airflow). Thermal failures often show up at *high ambient + mid-load + poor airflow*, not necessarily full-load.
- **Switching loss is often layout- and drive-dependent.** In simulation, sweep **gate resistor** and include **gate loop inductance** (even a few nH changes ringing and loss).
- **Use transient thermal impedance (Zθ(t))**, not only steady-state Rθ, for pulsed/step loads and startup.
- **Magnetics can dominate thermals.** Model inductor/transformer copper + core loss; validate with a temperature rise test (magnetics are frequently the real hotspot).
- **Calibrate with 1–2 measurements early.** One good measured switching waveform + one good thermal data point will dramatically improve your simulation confidence.
